rows: Occupational asthma can be caused by breathing substances that act as respiratory sensitisers.
Employers must assess exposure risks and prevent or adequately control exposure to asthmagens.
Substitution, enclosure and effective local exhaust ventilation should be considered before relying on respiratory protection.
Respiratory protective equipment must be suitable, correctly fitted and maintained where residual risk remains.
Health surveillance is required where workers are exposed to substances known to cause occupational asthma and risk remains.
Workers should receive information and training on hazards, controls and early symptoms.
Symptoms that improve away from work may indicate a work relationship and should be reported promptly.
A diagnosed occupational asthma case linked to significant or regular exposure to a known sensitiser can be reportable under RIDDOR.
Asthma diagnosis and work attribution require clinical and occupational evidence, not an industry label alone.
An address cannot verify the substance, exposure level, control performance or individual susceptibility.
COSHH and the Health and Safety at Work Act are central to controlling workplace exposure to biological agents.
Deliberate work means intentionally handling, propagating, processing or manipulating biological agents as part of planned work.
Biological agents are classified into hazard groups according to their ability to cause human disease and other factors.
Risk assessment must consider the agent, hazard group, form, activity, exposure route and people at risk.
Laboratories and other contained work require appropriate containment measures to prevent worker exposure and environmental release.
Certain deliberate work with Hazard Group 2, 3 or 4 agents and consignment of Hazard Group 4 agents requires HSE notification or consent.
Records of workers exposed to specified agents and arrangements for incidents may be legally required.
Accidents that release an agent capable of causing severe human disease require immediate control and may require reporting.
Hazard-group classification indicates inherent hazard but does not by itself define the risk of a specific procedure.
Risk assessments must separately consider vulnerable workers, pregnancy, immunity, scale, equipment and containment performance.
Zoonoses are diseases carried by animals that can also affect humans.
COSHH requires employers and self-employed people to assess and control exposure to zoonotic microorganisms.
Controls should be maintained and workers must receive information, instruction and training.
Animal-contact attractions should provide adequate handwashing facilities with soap and running water.
Visitors should wash hands after animal contact and before eating or drinking.
Eating, drinking and hand-to-mouth activities should be separated from animal-contact areas.
Children require close supervision because they may be more vulnerable and have poorer hygiene awareness.
Manure, bedding, contaminated surfaces and footwear can transfer infectious material away from animal areas.
The presence of livestock does not prove that a specific zoonotic agent or human exposure is present.
Local conclusions require current animal-health, hygiene, environmental, clinical and laboratory evidence.
Scarlet fever is caused by group A Streptococcus bacteria.
Prompt antibiotic treatment reduces complications and onward transmission.
Children should not return to nursery or school, and adults should not return to work, until at least 24 hours after starting antibiotics.
Suspected scarlet-fever outbreaks should be reported promptly to the UKHSA health protection team.
Where diagnosis is uncertain, throat swabs may be collected before antibiotics are started.
Invasive group A streptococcal infection is uncommon but can cause severe disease.
Health protection teams assess contacts and can recommend preventive antibiotics for eligible higher-risk contacts.
UKHSA surveillance tracks scarlet fever and invasive group A streptococcal activity.
Regional or national surveillance does not prove transmission in a particular school, workplace or home.
Case and outbreak conclusions require current clinical, microbiological, contact and health-protection evidence.
